skill.title: Prove an inequality by induction
skill.input: inequality in n with starting value
needs: Prove a series identity by induction

steps.title: State what is to be proved

lines.text: Let $P(n)$ be the statement $3^n \ge 4n+1$, for $n \ge 2$.
So $P(2)$ is true.
Assume $3^k \ge 4k+1$ for some $k \ge 2$.

steps.title: Step 3: write down what P(k+1) says

lines.text: So $12k+3 > 4k+5$ for $k \ge 2$.
So $P(k+1)$ is true whenever $P(k)$ is true.
$P(2)$ is true, and $P(k)$ true implies $P(k+1)$ true. By induction, $P(n)$ is true for all $n \ge 2$, $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

skill.title: Prove √2 is irrational by contradiction
needs: Use equivalence, "if and only if" and proof by contradiction
Express a number as a product of primes

lines.text: Suppose $\sqrt{2}$ is rational.
Then $\sqrt{2} = \frac{p}{q}$ with $p, q$ integers having no common factor (the fraction is in simplest form).
$p^2$ is even (it equals $2q^2$), so $p$ is even. (The square of an odd number is odd.)
So $p = 2k$ for some integer $k$.
$q^2$ is even, so $q$ is even. So $q = 2m$ for some integer $m$.
$p$ and $q$ now have a common factor of $2$. This contradicts the assumption that they have no common factor.
So the assumption is false.
Assume $\sqrt{2}$ is rational, so $\sqrt{2} = \frac{a}{b}$ with $a, b \in \mathbb{Z}$, $b \neq 0$, and $\text{HCF}(a, b) = 1$.

steps.title: Square both sides and clear the fraction

lines.text: $a^2 = 2b^2$ is even, so $a^2$ is even.
The square of an odd number is odd, so $a$ must be even.

steps.title: Substitute a = 2k to show b is even

lines.text: So $b^2$ is even, and therefore $b$ is even.
Both $a$ and $b$ are even, so they share the factor $2$.
This contradicts $\text{HCF}(a, b) = 1$, so $\sqrt{2}$ is not rational.

skill.title: Integrate powers, sums and constant multiples
skill.example: ∫(3x² − 4x) dx → x³ − 2x² + c; ∫√x dx → ⅔x^(3/2) + c
needs: Write an expression as a power of a base

steps.title: Integrate each term: add 1 to the power, divide by the new power

lines.text: Use $\int x^n\,dx = \frac{x^{n+1}}{n+1}$.
Raise the power by 1 and divide by the new power: $\int x^n\,dx = \frac{x^{n+1}}{n+1} + c$.
